definition.text: Conservation finance is raising and managing money to protect land, water and natural resources.

facts.text: It draws on public, private and nonprofit money, using tools from loans and grants to tax breaks and market-based mechanisms, at local to national scales.
Conservation has traditionally been paid for by donations, foundation grants and government money such as tax incentives, ballot measures, bonds and agency budgets.

It is sometimes set apart from fundraising: fundraising gathers money that is never paid back, while conservation finance uses a wider set of financial tools to mobilise and manage capital for conservation results.
Its supporters argue that public and charitable funding falls far short of global needs; one widely cited estimate put yearly needs in the hundreds of billions of dollars, far above actual flows.
To close that gap it tries to add money from financial markets, through debt financing, tax benefits, private equity and project finance.
Early tools were debt-for-nature swaps in the 1980s, followed by incentive-based approaches such as payments for ecosystem services.
By the mid-2000s it was described as a distinct field, and recent analyses stress drawing in private capital through labelled bonds and blended finance.
Deals are usually built around an identifiable source of cash flow or budget authority that can pay for conservation over time.

title: Sources of conservation capital
article: Conservation finance#Sources of capital and actors

definition.text: Money for nature comes from domestic public spending, international public finance including aid, and private spending and investment.

facts.text: Market-rate capital can come from private investors and from public or charitable investors working through development finance institutions and multilateral development banks.
Conservation NGOs and foundations often act as go-betweens that implement projects.
Because NGOs receive much of their income from governments and foundations, adding up total conservation finance risks counting the same money twice.
Public and charitable money is sometimes described as catalytic: covering early costs or sharing risk so that private investment follows.

definition.text: A conservation trust fund is a long-term fund that gives grants to conservation work, often set up as an endowment or a fund spent down over time.

facts.text: They help pay for managing protected areas, including the running costs that short-term grants struggle to cover.
Experience with debt-for-nature swaps helped shape later tools such as conservation trust funds.

definition.text: Three tests of whether paid-for conservation really works: whether the result would not have happened anyway, whether harm simply moves elsewhere, and whether gains last.

facts.text: Additionality asks whether a financed action achieves conservation that would not have happened without the payment.
Leakage, or spillover, is when protecting one place pushes damaging activity to another, cutting the net benefit.

Permanence worries arise where results depend on people keeping to agreements over long periods; durability depends on contract length, enforcement, land pressures and whether behaviour persists after payments stop.
Setting baselines and counterfactuals is hard in practice, which weakens claims of additionality and impact.

definition.text: The costs of finding, assembling, checking, contracting and monitoring conservation projects, often cited as a barrier to scaling up.

facts.text: These costs bite hardest where projects are small, varied or need intensive monitoring and verification.
They can make projects less investable and raise the cost of capital.
Debt-for-nature swaps, for example, need coordination among debtor governments, creditors and NGOs.

title: Measuring conservation finance results

definition.text: Conservation finance deals often require reporting both how money was spent and what ecological results it achieved.

facts.text: Reports may separate outputs, such as area under management, from outcomes, such as changes in ecological condition.
The Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures recommends reporting nature-related dependencies and impacts, though data gaps limit consistency.
Payment schemes also raise equity questions: who can be paid, how schemes affect land tenure and livelihoods, and whether wealthier landholders benefit most.

definition.text: Sustainable finance covers the practices, standards, rules and products that seek financial returns while weighing environmental, social and governance concerns.

facts.text: It is often used as a synonym for ESG investing, but the wider field also includes impact investing, social finance and ethical investing.
The Paris Agreement asks parties to make finance flows consistent with low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development.
It is described as a cornerstone for reaching the UN Sustainable Development Goals, adopted in 2015 with 17 goals and 169 targets.
Green, social and sustainability bonds and sustainability-linked bonds together reached $170 billion in 2018 and $653.5 billion in 2025.
Public finance stays important, but much of the money for climate goals is expected to come from the private sector.
Over two decades it grew from a niche topic into a recognised field of research and university teaching.

definition.text: UNEP separates three nested terms often used as synonyms: climate finance, green finance and sustainable finance.

facts.text: Climate finance mainly funds adaptation, resilience, mitigation and a just transition.
Green finance covers climate finance plus other environmental issues such as protecting biodiversity.
Sustainable finance adds social and governance concerns, making it the broadest term for finance that supports sustainable development.
One review traces three periods: forerunners from the 1970s to 2010, an early phase from 2010 to 2021, and a mature phase since 2021.

title: Sustainable finance taxonomy

definition.text: A taxonomy is an official classification that says which economic activities count as green or sustainable for investors.

facts.text: The European Commission set up a technical expert group in 2018 to define such a classification, and the EU taxonomy came into force in July 2020.
Its aim is to prevent greenwashing and help investors make greener choices.
Investments are judged against six objectives: climate mitigation, climate adaptation, the circular economy, pollution, water and biodiversity.
Classing fossil gas and nuclear energy as sustainable proved controversial, with some expert advisers threatening to resign over gas.
Mongolia adopted a national green finance taxonomy in 2018, among the first countries to do so.

contested_note: Whether fossil gas and nuclear power belong in the EU taxonomy is disputed.

definition.text: Rules and standards that ask companies to report climate and other sustainability risks and impacts so investors can judge them.

facts.text: The Financial Stability Board launched the Taskforce on Climate-related Financial Disclosures in 2015 to push firms to report climate risks and how they govern them.
Research shows disclosure policies have limited effect when they stay voluntary.
The EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, adopted in October 2022, widens coverage to about 50,000 companies from about 11,700.

title: Green central banking

definition.text: Green central banking is the idea that central banks should use monetary policy and capital rules to help cut emissions and steer money to green investment.

facts.text: In 2018 eight central banks created the Network for Greening the Financial System, which has grown to nearly 116 central banks and supervisors.
Banks have proposed a lighter 'green-supporting factor' on capital rules, while central bankers and nonprofits prefer heavier capital charges on fossil-fuel assets.
Many researchers argue that pursuing such goals strains the legitimacy of independent central banks, whose mandates rarely include climate aims.

contested_note: Researchers dispute whether independent central banks may legitimately pursue climate goals.

definition.text: Sustainable finance lacks a single accepted standard for measuring and reporting sustainability, so companies and funds are hard to compare.

facts.text: Many bodies write reporting standards independently, including the GRI, the IFRS Foundation and the Carbon Disclosure Project, which has confused companies and investors.
One paper found ESG ratings agree only 60% of the time, against 99% for credit ratings from the largest agencies.
This spread is called the ESG ratings gap or 'aggregate confusion'.
Because standards vary and change, some funds labelled ESG still hold oil and coal shares.
